newsitem.title: USA: Minor U.S. presidential candidates keep on plugging.
newsitem.headline: Minor U.S. presidential candidates keep on plugging.

text.p: They're an odd lot, but they all have one thing in common with Bill Clinton and Bob Dole -- they want to live in the White House.

Besides the Democratic president and the Republican challenger, about 270 men and women have announced they are running for U.S. president, according to the Federal Election Commission, which tracks such things.
Only 21 including Clinton and Dole are on the ballot in at least one of the 50 states or the District of Columbia for the Nov. 5 election, the FEC said.
Ross Perot, nominee of his self-created Reform Party, the best known of these minor party candidates, is on all the ballots along with Clinton and Dole.

The only other candidate who can make that boast is Harry Browne, nominee of the Libertarian Party which demands maximum individual freedom and minimum government. Browne, 63, is a Franklin, Tennessee, investment adviser who charges $500 for an hour's worth of advice.

Many voters know the positions of the major candidates but the smaller-party nominees like Browne -- and even Perot, who was shut out of the two presidential debates -- have a tough time getting free television time to air their messages.

Some candidates do take what many would consider extreme stands. Clinton, for instance, says "the era of big government is over" and Dole wants even less, but Browne wants almost no government at all. He says federal powers should be limited to what is literally listed in the U.S. Constitution, such as providing for the national defence.

He would have the mother of all yard-sales and sell off everything from national parks like the Grand Canyon to federal buildings. He would not just overhaul the Internal Revenue Service as Dole promises, but abolish it.

Another contender with fairly widespread exposure is John Hagelin, 42, of Fairfield, Iowa, a Harvard-trained physicist on 44 state ballots as the Natural Law Party candidate. He ran four years ago and got 39,163 votes.

Hagelin, closely associated with the Transcendental Meditation movement, practices what is called "yogic flying," according to an aide. Practitioners say it is levitation. Others call it hopping into the air from a sitting position.
Hagelin's campaign platform centres on a promise to "bring the nation back into harmony with natural law -- with the fundamental laws that govern and administer life."
Howard Phillips of the conservative Taxpayers Party is another presidential veteran who got 43,398 votes in 1992 and is on 39 ballots.

Consumer advocate Ralph Nader is running an unorthodox, low-key presidential campaign in which he refuses to spend more than $5,000 as nominee of the environmentalist Green Party. Nader is on 22 ballots.
Colorado voters will have the biggest choice this year with 13 presidential candidates on its ballot. Utah has 12 and Minnesota and Arizona offer 11.
